title: The many faces of Indra
description: From Devanagari to Unicode: why Indra is more than a domain name.
author: PuniCodex Team
body:
# The many faces of Indra

No important name has only one face. **Indra** appears as ​a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each face in ‌turn: the name and its roots, the Devanagari original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored spelling resolve in ‌a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *indra* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored ​name:** Indra
- **ASCII form:** indra
- **Meaning:** "the god of the atmosphere and sky"
- **Domain of influence:** Storms, War, Kingship
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** इन्द्र (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Indra** (*indra*) — ​The Storm, the Vajra, King of the Gods · the god of the atmosphere and sky — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Storms, War, Kingship". ​The name means "the god of the atmosphere and sky".

**Indra** is the king of the Vedic gods: the thunderbolt-bearer who slew the dragon Vritra and released the rivers, the drinker of ​soma who roars into battle, the thousand-eyed lord of the sky. Two hundred and fifty hymns of the Rigveda are addressed to him — more than to any other deity — making ​him the best-documented god of the ancient world.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Indra** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/indra/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed ‌form itself. The plain ASCII form *indra* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically ​complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **इन्द्र**. Etymologically it means "the god of the atmosphere and sky".

The ASCII form *indra* survives only because the early domain-name system ​could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Indra** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **i** → **I** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **d** → **d** — Same
- **r** ​→ **r** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Short /a/

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **इन्द्र**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Indra*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- ‌Sanskrit Indra is written in Devanagari as इन्द्र
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex ​articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈɪndrə/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Indra).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **In-** — Short i as in “bit”, followed by the retroflex ‌dental n — tongue curled back.
- **-dra** — The d is retroflex ḍ in careful speech; the final a is a light schwa, half-sounded.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ​“IN-druh” — the final vowel breathes rather than lands

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Vedic** — Índra
- **Pāli/Prakrit** — Inda
- **Buddhist** — Śakra

One of the oldest named gods in ​any Indo-European language — the name appears already in the Rigveda’s first hymn.

## Mythology

The Indra of the Rigveda is a storm in divine form: mighty, boisterous, sometimes embarrassed, always central. ​His one great myth — the combat with Vritra — is the Vedic creation story: the waters of life imprisoned by the dragon, the thunderbolt that splits the mountains, the rivers released. ​Everything else in his mythology is commentary on that victory.

### The Slaying of Vritra (Rigveda 1.32)

Vritra, the “Enveloper”, coiled about the world’s waters and held them fast in his mountain caves. ​Indra, armed with the vajra forged by Tvashtri from Dadhichi’s bones, struck the dragon on its flank; the waters burst free and flooded to the sea. ‘Like lowing cows the waters rushed’ ‌— the oldest dragon-slaying in recorded literature, and the template for every one after it.

### The Drink of Soma (Rigveda 8)

Before the combat, Indra drinks three lakes of soma pressed by ​the priests; filled with the draught, his strength is irresistible and his belly vast. The hymns taunt and flatter him by turns — the Vedic poets knew their storm-god was vain, and ‌loved him for it. Soma is both his fuel and his fee.

### The Intoxication Hymn (Rigveda 10.119)

The most human hymn in the Rigveda: Indra speaks in the first person, drunk on ​soma, boasting — ‘I will break the earth’s two halves apart, like a gourd I will break the two worlds’. The gods’ king, for one hymn, sounds like a warrior at the ‌feast, and the poets let him.

### From King of Gods to Dethroned Elder (Epic & Purāṇic Cycle)

In the later epics the balance shifts: Vishnu’s avatars take the great victories, and ​Indra becomes the anxious king who sins — the seducer of Ahalyā, the raider of Triparu, the god who must yield his throne’s preeminence. The Purāṇas preserve a dignity-muted Indra, still lord ‌of the eastern quarter and of the storm, but no longer the cosmos’ protagonist.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Indra concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a ​compressed statement about the name:

- **The Vajra** — The thunderbolt forged from the bones of the sage Dadhichi — Indra’s irresistible weapon against the dragon.
- **Slayer of Vritra** — He split the ‌dragon that held the waters captive, and the rivers ran free — the founding victory of cosmic order.
- **Lord of Soma** — The sacred draught that makes gods gods: Indra drinks the ​soma press before every battle.
- **The Thousand-Eyed** — His body bears a thousand eyes — the marks of the gods’ curse and his redemption; the sky’s innumerable lights.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The ​material record for Indra survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

‌No Indra temples survive in India — the Vedic cult was fire and libation, not image. But his name is carved across Southeast Asia: the seventh-century Sanskrit inscriptions of Cambodia invoke him ‌as royal ancestor, and Borobudur’s reliefs show Śakra attending the Buddha.

## Realm & Domain

**Indra** is the king of the Vedic gods: the thunderbolt-bearer who slew the dragon Vritra and released the ‌rivers, the drinker of soma who roars into battle, the thousand-eyed lord of the sky. Two hundred and fifty hymns of the Rigveda are addressed to him — more than to ​any other deity — making him the best-documented god of the ancient world.

### The Vajra

The thunderbolt forged from the bones of the sage Dadhichi — Indra’s irresistible weapon against the dragon.

### ​Slayer of Vritra

He split the dragon that held the waters captive, and the rivers ran free — the founding victory of cosmic order.

### Lord of Soma

The sacred draught that makes ‌gods gods: Indra drinks the soma press before every battle.

### The Thousand-Eyed

His body bears a thousand eyes — the marks of the gods’ curse and his redemption; the sky’s innumerable lights.

## ​Across Cultures

In Buddhism Indra becomes Śakra, lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, subservient to the Buddha and guardian of the dharma — the storm-god converted into a devotee. In Jainism he is ​a class of heaven-rulers. Greek observers heard Zeus in him; modern comparative philology confirmed the kinship: Indra and Zeus descend from the same Proto-Indo-European sky-father’s thunderbolt.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index include [[thor|Þórr]] (thunder sovereignty), [[zeus|Zeús]] (thunder sovereignty), [[adad|Adad]] (thunder / storm sovereignty), [[baal|Baꜥal]] (thunder / storm sovereignty), [[enlil|Enlīl]] (thunder / storm sovereignty), and [[illapa|Illapa]] (thunder / storm sovereignty).

## Cultural Legacy

He ​is embedded in the oldest Indo-European poetry extant — every study of dragon-slaying, thunder-gods, or soma/haoma ritual begins with him. The word ‘Indra’ entered Southeast Asian royal names (Indravarman, Indrapura) carried by ​Hindu expansion; and the Vajra passed east into Tibetan Buddhism as the thunderbolt-sceptre of the vajrayāna itself.

The account of Indra given in this edition rests on the witnesses ‌and reference works listed below. Lexica and etymological dictionaries secure the form and meaning of the name; the literary and religious texts supply the narrative evidence.

## A Meditation

Indra: a name with no diacritics because it never ‌needed any — the retroflex consonants of the Vedic hymns sit quietly inside plain letters, as they have since the first singer pressed soma. To restore him in ASCII is to hand ​the thunderbolt back to the oldest god who still answers to the spelling a schoolchild would guess.

## The Unicode Restoration

Myth, script, sound, cult, legacy, domain: the faces of Indra add up to a single argument — that a ‌name is a record, and records deserve fidelity. But fallback is not identity. **Indra** is the name; everything else is a convenience.

## A Closer Look at ​the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Indra**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in ​Devanagari rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *indra* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the ​public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, ‌the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **i**, **n**, **d**, **r**, **a** — ​so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and ​addressable.

## Indra in Its Tradition

**Indra** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is counted among 102 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Storms, War, ​Kingship — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in ‌the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Indra**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That ​catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a ​trend. **Indra** is one such vote.

## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Indra** resolves, ​it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone ‌who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in ​an article while the public web flattened it to *indra*. Now the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains ‌compatible while the visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not a single ‌decision; it is a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Indra**, the chain begins with the attested form in Devanagari, continues through the standard scholarly ​romanizations, and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "the god of the atmosphere and sky" anchors the name in its semantic field; without that anchor, the ​marks would float free of the figure they name. The restored form **Indra** and the ASCII form *indra* share the same Latin letters; the restoration here is a conventional capitalization rather than ​a recovery of lost diacritics or special characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears openly: Indra aSCII-equivalent form. The rule is mechanical, not ​editorial, which means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence produced it, because every step ‌is recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
